blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Simple linear regression fits a straight line between one continuous predictor x and one continuous outcome y: ŷ = b₀ + b₁x, where ŷ (“y-hat”) is the predicted outcome, b₀ the intercept and b₁ the slope.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: This is the simplest regression model: the “best” straight line through a scatter diagram (recall §4.4), where “best” has the exact meaning given in §12.2.2. The equation has just two numbers to interpret: where the line crosses the y-axis, and how steeply it rises.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: For the 100 children aged 12 to 36 months in the clinic register, the fitted line is predicted weight (kg) = 8.5 + 0.15 × age (months). Each extra month of age adds 0.15 kg to the predicted weight. At age 0 the equation gives 8.5 kg, but no child younger than 12 months was measured, so that value is an extrapolation with no biological meaning (§12.2.3). The figure therefore draws the line only over the observed ages.

blocks.alt: The least-squares regression line for weight on age
blocks.caption: Figure 12.1. The least-squares line for weight on age in the clinic register, drawn over the observed ages (12–36 months) only. The line passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ); the red segment is child C031’s residual (§12.2.1).

points.html: Look at the scatter diagram before fitting (recall §4.4). A straight line fitted to a curved relationship over-predicts in some parts of the range and under-predicts in others (§12.4.5 shows how to model curves).

blocks.html: The Regression Model – Population, Sample, and Error

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A regression equation is a model of how the outcome arises in the population: Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε, where β₀ and β₁ are fixed, unknown population parameters and ε is a random error term holding everything that affects the outcome other than the predictor. The line fitted to a sample, ŷ = b₀ + b₁x, gives estimates b₀ and b₁ of those parameters.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
For a straight line to describe children’s weights perfectly, every child of a given age would have to weigh exactly the same. They don’t: genetics, nutrition, illness and ordinary individual variation all matter. So the honest model is not “weight equals a line” but “weight equals a line plus everything else”. That “everything else” is ε, and it is an expected part of the model, not a defect in it.

This is the parameter-versus-statistic distinction of Chapter 1 again (recall §1.3). There is a true intercept β₀ and a true slope β₁ for the whole population, fixed and unobservable. From one sample you calculate b₀ and b₁. Greek letters for what is true and unknown; Roman letters for what you calculated. Another sample of children would give a slightly different b₁, while β₁ never moves. Because b₁ is an estimate of β₁, it carries uncertainty, which §12.2.4 quantifies.

Two terms follow:

  • The fitted value ŷ is the model’s prediction for an observation: the height of the line at that observation’s x.
  • The residual is observed y − fitted ŷ. It is the calculable stand-in for the unobservable ε.

ε belongs to the population model and can never be observed. A residual belongs to your sample and can be calculated for every data point, which is why residuals are the main diagnostic tool (§12.5).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Child C031 in the register is 18 months old and weighs 11.8 kg. The fitted model is ŷ = 8.5 + 0.15x.

  • Fitted value: ŷ = 8.5 + (0.15 × 18) = 11.2 kg, the model’s prediction for any 18-month-old.
  • Observed value: 11.8 kg.
  • Residual: 11.8 − 11.2 = +0.6 kg. This child is 0.6 kg heavier than the model expected.

That 0.6 kg is not a mistake. It is this child being an individual. The model never claimed every 18-month-old weighs 11.2 kg; it claimed 11.2 kg is the average around which 18-month-olds vary.

points.html: Population model: Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε. Fitted sample model: ŷ = b₀ + b₁x.
β₀ and β₁ are parameters (fixed, unknown). b₀ and b₁ are statistics (calculated, varying from sample to sample).
Residual = observed − fitted. Every assumption check in §12.3 and §12.5 is done on residuals, because they are the observable counterpart of ε.

blocks.html: Least Squares Principle

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The least squares principle chooses the line that minimises the sum of squared residuals, SSE = Σ(yᵢ − b₀ − b₁xᵢ)², over all possible values of b₀ and b₁.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Infinitely many lines could be drawn through a scatter of points. For any candidate line, measure each point’s vertical distance from it, square each distance, and add them up. The least-squares line is the one line that makes this total as small as possible. Squaring does what it did for the variance (recall §3.6): a point above the line and one equally far below both count, instead of cancelling, and large misses are penalised more than small ones.

Two sums do all the work. For n pairs (xᵢ, yᵢ) with means x̄ and ȳ:

Sxx = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² Sxy = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ)

Sxx is the numerator of the variance of x, and Sxy is the numerator of the covariance of x and y (recall §11.2).

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
1. SSE is a smooth bowl-shaped function of b₀ and b₁. At its lowest point its slope in each direction is zero.
  2. Slope with respect to b₀: −2Σ(yᵢ − b₀ − b₁xᵢ) = 0. Divide by −2n: ȳ − b₀ − b₁x̄ = 0, so b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄.
  3. Substitute this b₀ into SSE: each residual becomes (yᵢ − ȳ) − b₁(xᵢ − x̄).
  4. Slope with respect to b₁: −2Σ(xᵢ − x̄)[(yᵢ − ȳ) − b₁(xᵢ − x̄)] = 0, so Sxy − b₁Sxx = 0, and b₁ = Sxy ÷ Sxx.
  5. Pearson’s r is Sxy ÷ √(Sxx·Syy) (recall §11.2), and the SDs are s_x = √(Sxx/(n−1)) and s_y = √(Syy/(n−1)). Therefore b₁ = r × s_y ÷ s_x.

Three properties follow at once:

  • The line passes through the mean point. Step 2 says ȳ = b₀ + b₁x̄: at x = x̄ the line predicts exactly ȳ.
  • The slope has the sign of r, because s_y ÷ s_x is always positive. b₁ = 0 exactly when r = 0.
  • Regression to the mean. Rewrite the line as ŷ − ȳ = r(s_y/s_x)(x − x̄), then divide by s_y: (ŷ − ȳ)/s_y = r × (x − x̄)/s_x. In SD units, the prediction is r times as far from the mean as the predictor. Unless |r| = 1, predictions are pulled towards the mean (§12.1).

Step 2 also shows that the residuals sum to zero: Σ(yᵢ − b₀ − b₁xᵢ) = 0.

Illustration / Example: Worked Calculation (clinic register, n = 100)

  1. x̄ = 24.35 months, ȳ = 12.15 kg; Sxx = 6190.8 months², Sxy = 928.6 kg·months.
  2. b₁ = 928.6 ÷ 6190.8 = 0.150 kg per month.
  3. Check through r: s_x = 7.91 months, s_y = 1.45 kg, r = 0.820, so r × s_y ÷ s_x = 0.820 × 1.446 ÷ 7.908 = 0.150. Same answer.
  4. b₀ = 12.15 − 0.150 × 24.35 = 12.15 − 3.65 = 8.50 kg.
  5. Mean point: 8.50 + 0.150 × 24.35 = 12.15 kg = ȳ.
  6. In SD units: a 36-month-old is (36 − 24.35) ÷ 7.91 = 1.47 SD above the mean age. The predicted weight, 8.50 + 0.150 × 36 = 13.90 kg, is (13.90 − 12.15) ÷ 1.446 = 1.21 SD above the mean weight, which is 0.82 × 1.47.

points.html: b₁ = Sxy/Sxx = r·s_y/s_x and b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄. Every software package computes these (for several predictors, the same principle solved with matrix algebra, which is beyond this book).
The fitted line always passes through (x̄, ȳ). This is a quick check on a hand-computed line.
Least squares is a rule for choosing the line. It needs no assumption about the distribution of ε. The assumptions of §12.3 are needed for the standard errors, CIs and p-values of §12.2.4.

questions.prompt: For the clinic register, Sxy = 928.6, Sxx = 6190.8, x̄ = 24.35 months and ȳ = 12.15 kg. Compute b₁ and b₀. Then find the fitted weight and the residual for a 30-month-old child who weighs 12.0 kg.
questions.answer: b₁ = Sxy ÷ Sxx = 928.6 ÷ 6190.8 = 0.150 kg per month. b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄ = 12.15 − 0.150 × 24.35 = 12.15 − 3.65 = 8.50 kg. Fitted weight at 30 months: 8.50 + 0.150 × 30 = 8.50 + 4.50 = 13.00 kg. Residual = observed − fitted = 12.0 − 13.0 = −1.0 kg: this child is 1 kg lighter than the model predicts for her age.

questions.prompt: Children in a school are weighed, and the 20 thinnest are enrolled in a feeding programme. Three months later their mean BMI z-score has risen. Name one reason, other than the programme, why their mean would rise, and one design feature that would remove it.
questions.answer: Regression to the mean: the 20 were selected because their first measurement was extreme, and part of that extremeness was measurement error and short-term fluctuation (a recent illness, a measurement slip), which is not repeated at the second weighing. Their mean would move towards the population mean even with no programme. (Normal growth and seasonal change are further reasons.) A randomised control group chosen in the same way (thinnest children, half not fed) regresses by the same amount, so the programme’s effect is the difference between groups. Selecting on the mean of two baseline measurements also reduces the problem.

questions.prompt: Two variables have r = 0.5. A person is 2 SD above the mean of x. How many SDs above the mean of y is the predicted value?
questions.answer: In SD units the prediction is r times the predictor: (ŷ − ȳ)/s_y = r × (x − x̄)/s_x = 0.5 × 2 = 1.0 SD above the mean of y.

blocks.html: Interpreting Slope and Intercept

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The slope b₁ is the expected change in the outcome for a one-unit increase in the predictor. The intercept b₀ is the predicted outcome when the predictor equals zero.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: These two numbers carry the real-world meaning of the line. Interpreting them in the units of the actual variables is the most practical skill in reading regression output.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In “predicted weight (kg) = 8.5 + 0.15 × age (months)”, the slope means that, on average across the sampled children, each additional month of age goes with 0.15 kg more predicted weight (1.8 kg per year). The intercept, 8.5 kg, is the predicted weight at age 0. No child younger than 12 months was measured, so this number only positions the line; it is not an estimate of birth weight.

points.html: A slope’s units are (units of outcome) per (unit of predictor). “0.15” alone means nothing; “0.15 kg per month” does.

The intercept is meaningful only when x = 0 lies within, or close to, the observed range. Extrapolating beyond the data assumes the relationship stays linear where it was never observed. To give the intercept meaning, centre the predictor: with age − 24 months as x, b₀ becomes the predicted weight of a 24-month-old (8.50 + 0.150 × 24 = 12.1 kg).
The slope has the sign of Pearson’s r and is zero exactly when r is zero (§12.2.2). The slope carries units; r does not.

blocks.html: Coefficient Standard Error, Confidence Interval and p-value

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Because b₁ estimates an unknown parameter, it has a sampling distribution. Its standard error SE(b₁) is the standard deviation of that distribution. Its 95% confidence interval is b₁ ± t × SE(b₁). Its p-value tests H₀: β₁ = 0, the hypothesis that the predictor has no linear association with the outcome. All three rest on the standard error of the estimate (the residual standard error), s = √[SSE/(n − 2)], which estimates σ, the SD of ε.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Every idea here was built earlier. It is four familiar steps applied to b₁.

Step one: the scatter around the line. Before asking how precise the slope is, ask how far points typically fall from the line. SSE is the total squared miss; divide by its degrees of freedom and take the square root: s = √[SSE/(n − 2)]. The divisor is n − 2, not n − 1, because two parameters (b₀ and b₁) were estimated from the data before the residuals could be computed (recall the degrees-of-freedom logic of §3.6). s is in the outcome’s units. With roughly Normal residuals, about 95% of individuals lie within about ±2s of the line.

Step two: b₁ varies, and its spread is SE(b₁). Another sample of children would give a slightly different b₁. The SD of those b₁ values across repeated samples is its standard error (recall §6.7). It answers: if I repeated the study, how much would the slope move?

Step three: the confidence interval. As in Chapter 7, the 95% CI is estimate ± (critical value × SE): b₁ ± t × SE(b₁), with t from the t-distribution on n − k − 1 degrees of freedom (n observations, k predictors, one more for the intercept). The interval is the range of slopes compatible with the data. The 95% belongs to the procedure: intervals built this way capture β₁ in 95% of repeated samples. It is not a 95% probability that β₁ lies in this particular interval (recall §7.2).

Step four: the test. H₀: β₁ = 0 says the true line is flat. The test statistic counts how many SEs b₁ sits from zero, t = b₁ ÷ SE(b₁), compared with the same t-distribution (recall §8.5). The CI and the p-value are two views of one calculation: a 95% CI that excludes zero goes with p < 0.05.

Derivation (why SE(b₁) = s ÷ √Sxx)

  1. Because Σ(xᵢ − x̄) = 0, Sxy = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)yᵢ. So b₁ = Σ wᵢyᵢ with weights wᵢ = (xᵢ − x̄)/Sxx: a weighted sum of the outcomes.
  2. Treat the x values as fixed. If the yᵢ are independent, each with variance σ² about the line, then Var(b₁) = Σ wᵢ²σ² (recall §6.5: variances of independent quantities add, and a constant multiplier comes out squared).
  3. Σ wᵢ² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/Sxx² = Sxx/Sxx² = 1/Sxx. So Var(b₁) = σ²/Sxx and SD(b₁) = σ/√Sxx.
  4. σ is unknown, so it is estimated by s: SE(b₁) = s ÷ √Sxx. Because σ is estimated, the t-distribution replaces the Normal (recall §5.7.2.3).

The formula shows the three things that shrink SE(b₁): a smaller s (less scatter around the line), a larger n, and a wider spread of x (both make Sxx larger). A study of children aged 12 to 36 months estimates the age–weight slope far more precisely than one of 17- to 19-month-olds, because a short lever is harder to angle accurately than a long one.

Illustration / Example: Worked Calculation (clinic register)

  1. SSE = 67.81 kg², n − 2 = 98. s = √(67.81 ÷ 98) = √0.692 = 0.83 kg. Individual children typically sit within about ±1.7 kg (2 × 0.83) of the line.
  2. √Sxx = √6190.8 = 78.68. SE(b₁) = 0.832 ÷ 78.68 = 0.011 kg per month.
  3. t = 0.14999 ÷ 0.01057 = 14.19 on 98 df (with the rounded SE, 0.150 ÷ 0.011 ≈ 14). p < 0.001.
  4. t₉₈ for 95% = 1.984. CI = 0.150 ± 1.984 × 0.0106 = 0.150 ± 0.021 = 0.129 to 0.171 kg per month.
Predictor Coefficient Std. Error t p-value 95% CI
Age (months) 0.150 0.011 14.19 <0.001 0.129 to 0.171

Reading it: for each additional month of age, predicted weight rises by 0.15 kg. With an SE of 0.011, slopes around 0.14 or 0.16 would be unremarkable in a repeat of the study. The estimate sits about 14 SEs from zero, so p < 0.001. The data are compatible with true slopes from about 0.13 to 0.17 kg per month, that is, a monthly gain of about 130 to 170 grams. “p < 0.001” says only that zero is incompatible with the data; the interval gives a range a paediatrician can judge as important or trivial.

Two different intervals at x = 18 months. The confidence interval for the mean weight of all 18-month-olds uses SE = s√[1/n + (x − x̄)²/Sxx] = 0.832 × √[0.01 + 0.0065] = 0.107 kg: 11.20 ± 1.984 × 0.107 = 10.99 to 11.41 kg. The prediction interval for one new 18-month-old adds the child’s own scatter, SE = s√[1 + 1/n + (x − x̄)²/Sxx] = 0.839 kg: 11.20 ± 1.984 × 0.839 = 9.54 to 12.86 kg. The first narrows as n grows; the second can never be narrower than about ±2s.

points.html: s = √[SSE/(n − k − 1)] (n − 2 in simple regression): the typical distance of a point from the line, in outcome units. SE(b₁) = s/√Sxx in simple regression.
95% CI: b₁ ± t(n−k−1) × SE(b₁). Test: t = b₁ ÷ SE(b₁) for H₀: β₁ = 0.
Report the CI, not only the p-value: it shows the size of the effects compatible with the data.
A statistically significant coefficient is not automatically an important one. With a large sample, a clinically negligible slope can reach a tiny p-value (recall §8.5).
A non-significant coefficient does not show that the predictor is unrelated to the outcome. A wide CI spanning zero means the study could not distinguish a meaningful association from none.
A prediction interval for an individual is always wider than the CI for the mean at the same x.

blocks.html: R-Squared

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: R-squared (R²) is the proportion of the total variation in the outcome that the regression model accounts for: R² = SSR ÷ SST = 1 − SSE ÷ SST, where SST = Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)² is the total sum of squares, SSE the residual sum of squares, and SSR = SST − SSE the regression (explained) sum of squares. It runs from 0 to 1.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
SST measures how much the children’s weights vary around their mean. After fitting the line, SSE is the variation left over around the line. The part that disappeared, SSR, is what age accounts for. This is the same partition of variation into parts that ANOVA uses (recall §9.5.1).

In simple regression, R² = r². Proof: SSR = Σ(ŷᵢ − ȳ)² = b₁²Sxx = (Sxy/Sxx)²Sxx = Sxy²/Sxx, so SSR/SST = Sxy²/(Sxx·Syy) = r².

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: For the clinic register, SST = 207.1, SSE = 67.8 and SSR = 139.3 kg². R² = 139.3 ÷ 207.1 = 0.67, and r² = 0.820² = 0.67 as well. About 67% of the variation in the children’s weights is accounted for by differences in their age. The remaining 33% reflects everything else: feeding, illness, genetics and ordinary individual variation.

blocks.alt: How R² splits the total variation in weight into explained and residual parts
blocks.caption: Figure 12.2. R² for the clinic regression of weight on age: of the total sum of squares (207.1 kg²), age accounts for 139.3 (67%) and 67.8 (33%) remains as residual.

blocks.html:
Adjusted R². Adding any predictor, even a column of random numbers, can only lower SSE, so plain R² can only rise. That makes plain R² useless for comparing models of different sizes. Adjusted R² replaces sums of squares with variance estimates:

adjusted R² = 1 − [SSE/(n − k − 1)] ÷ [SST/(n − 1)] = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − k − 1)

Derivation (when adjusted R² rises)

  1. SST/(n − 1) does not depend on the model, so adjusted R² rises exactly when s² = SSE/(n − k − 1) falls.
  2. Add one predictor. SSE falls by some amount Δ, and the residual df falls from d + 1 to d. Write SSE₁ for the new SSE.
  3. s² falls when SSE₁/d < (SSE₁ + Δ)/(d + 1). Multiply out: SSE₁ < dΔ, that is, Δ ÷ (SSE₁/d) > 1.
  4. Δ ÷ (SSE₁/d) is the partial F statistic for the new predictor. For a single added coefficient this statistic equals the square of that coefficient’s t statistic (an algebraic identity whose proof is beyond this book; it matches the distributional fact t² = F of §5.7.2.5). So adjusted R² rises if and only if the new predictor’s |t| > 1, and falls when the predictor does not earn its place.

The bar |t| > 1 is much lower than significance at 5% (|t| ≈ 2), so a rise in adjusted R² does not show that a predictor matters.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Clinic model: n = 100, k = 1, R² = 0.6726. Adjusted R² = 1 − 0.3274 × 99/98 = 1 − 0.3308 = 0.669.
  2. Add a column of random numbers as a second predictor (simulated noise). Its t = −0.68. R² rises to 0.674, but adjusted R² falls to 0.667, as step 4 predicts for |t| < 1.

points.html: R² = SSR/SST = 1 − SSE/SST. In simple regression R² = r².

R² measures statistical fit, not usefulness. A model with modest R² built on modifiable risk factors may matter more than a high-R² model built on age and sex alone. A modest R² can still go with a precisely estimated, important slope.
Use adjusted R² for any model with more than one predictor, and for comparing models of different size. It rises only when the new predictor’s |t| exceeds 1.

questions.prompt: A colleague adds a fourth predictor to a model and R² rises from 0.41 to 0.43. They conclude the new predictor is clinically important. What is the flaw, and what should they check instead?
questions.answer: Adding any predictor, even random numbers, can only lower SSE, so R² can only rise; the rise says nothing about importance. They should check adjusted R² (which rises only if the new predictor’s |t| exceeds 1, itself a low bar), and, above all, the new predictor’s coefficient and 95% CI in clinical units: is the size of the association compatible with the data large enough to matter?

questions.prompt: Explain, using the error term, why a fitted line almost never passes through every data point, even when the model is a good one.
questions.answer: The model is Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε. The error term ε holds everything that affects the outcome besides X: other causes, individual variation and measurement error. The line describes the average outcome at each x; individuals scatter around it by their own ε. A good model gets the average right; it was never meant to predict every individual exactly.

questions.prompt: A regression of haemoglobin (g/dL) on weeks of iron supplementation in 27 women gives b₁ = 0.12 g/dL per week, s = 0.9 g/dL and Sxx = 900 weeks². Compute SE(b₁), the t statistic and the 95% CI for β₁ (t₂₅ = 2.060). Is the result compatible with no linear association?
questions.answer: SE(b₁) = s ÷ √Sxx = 0.9 ÷ 30 = 0.03 g/dL per week. t = 0.12 ÷ 0.03 = 4.0 on 27 − 2 = 25 df. 95% CI = 0.12 ± 2.060 × 0.03 = 0.12 ± 0.062 = 0.058 to 0.182 g/dL per week. The interval excludes zero (p < 0.001, since |t| = 4.0 is far beyond 2.06), so the data are not compatible with a flat line; they are compatible with gains from about 0.06 to 0.18 g/dL per week.
